title: The American Millennial Manifesto
eyebrow: An independent publication by Henok Ghebrechristos
headline: The attitude of dominance.
The culture that teaches it.
description: The American Millennial Manifesto applies Digital Organism Theory to American culture: how dominance is learned, organized, transmitted, and revised.

home.overviewClaim: What we learn to endure can become what we ask of others.
home.overviewIntro: A work message interrupts dinner. A justified warning threatens a supervisor’s standing. Someone who once had little room to refuse begins setting terms for others. AMM follows these encounters through DOT: experience, interpretation, Intent, action, consequence, and what is carried into the next encounter.
home.overviewArgument: The Leech is the attitude that treats domination of other people as a legitimate route to security, worth, or advantage.
home.overviewSource: Chapter One · The Leech — The Attitude of Dominance
home.premise: AMM applies Digital Organism Theory to American culture: how fear, status, and inherited lessons can make control seem necessary; how institutions reinforce that attitude; and how people learn to carry it forward—or revise it.
home.conceptsLabel: How cultural instructions become everyday conduct

concepts.label: Worth
concepts.script: Your worth is what you earn.
concepts.text: A credential, salary, or promotion can become proof that a person deserves to belong. DOT calls the carried organization of such expectations the Painting. AMM asks when a local measure of performance becomes a verdict on a whole life.
concepts.argument: A skill can improve a task; it cannot establish that another person has lesser standing.
concepts.source: Chapter Three · The Host and the Infection

concepts.label: Fear
concepts.text: At dinner, a work message can carry a learned demand: answer now to remain indispensable. AMM distinguishes an expectation that can be questioned from a real employment threat that also requires material protection.
concepts.argument: If availability is treated as evidence of worth, another person's command of one's attention can feel like recognition.
concepts.source: Chapter Two · The Anatomy of Dominance

concepts.label: Authority
concepts.script: Being in charge means being right.
concepts.text: A warning can be heard as information about a task, or as a threat to the person holding authority. AMM examines how identifying with a role can turn a revisable decision into a demand that others remain silent.
concepts.argument: A role can be corrected without the person ceasing to exist.
concepts.source: Chapter One · The Leech — The Attitude of Dominance

concepts.label: Belonging
concepts.text: A group can provide care, memory, and solidarity. Its reputation can also become so bound to identity that criticism feels intolerable. AMM asks whether the same standard still applies when it reaches someone admired.
concepts.argument: A standard advertised as universal becomes conditional upon loyalty.
concepts.source: Chapter Three · The Host and the Infection

concepts.label: Transmission
concepts.script: I endured it. So should you.
concepts.text: A person once silenced becomes a supervisor. Their history can lead them to protect a colleague’s warning or teach silence as professionalism. In DOT, the resulting action becomes part of another person’s experience.
concepts.argument: There is a threshold between learning that one must sometimes endure a condition and learning that the condition is right to impose.
concepts.source: Chapter Three · The Host and the Infection

concepts.label: Revision
concepts.script: This is just how things are.
concepts.text: A new promise becomes credible through what happens next. A warning is protected, an error is corrected, a different response becomes affordable. Chapter Four follows how repeated encounters can revise expectations and Character.
concepts.argument: This is why cultural change requires consequences, not vocabulary alone.

home.scriptLabel: A cultural instruction examined by AMM
home.sceneAlt: The flag-patterned Host rests its head beside a laptop at a kitchen table, carrying the two-headed Leech. An untouched meal, household envelopes, keys, and a picture of a cow family in a green meadow surround it.
home.diagnosisTitle: How does an attitude become an arrangement?
home.diagnosisClaim: Dominance is learned, enacted, and reinforced.
home.diagnosisIntro: The Leech names an attitude of dominance. AMM examines how it can become organized in the Painting, expressed through Intent, and stabilized in Character. Institutions can give it reach by rewarding some choices and making others costly.
home.cureTitle: How can the next encounter be different?
home.cureIntro: Revision needs both a change in response and conditions that make another response possible: truthful interpretation, material support, accountable authority, and consequences that make a different practice credible.
home.cureStatus: A complete working chapter is included in the illustrated online edition. Version 1.1 is pending line editing.

deck: You keep the economy running. Who does it leave in control?
statement: The public is more than a resource.
approach: AMM follows the relationship between concentrated power, inherited culture, and everyday conduct. Its model asks how extraction becomes normal, who has room to refuse, and what makes correction possible.

analysis.title: How a system gets inside us.
analysis.description: Follow the relationship between institutions, inherited beliefs, and the decisions that keep an arrangement in place—or change it.
analysis.lineage: Inspired by DOT’s account of experience, interpretation, action, and consequence. AMM carries that process-oriented lens into public life.
analysis.evidence: The diagram organizes AMM’s argument. Particular claims still need evidence about authority, contribution, dependence, and transferred costs. An official source does not settle a claim by its status; a statistic needs its method, context, and limitations.

steps.label: Conditions
steps.title: Who sets the terms?
steps.description: Ownership, contracts, infrastructure, and law shape what people can access and what refusing will cost.
steps.question: Identify who controls the arrangement, who depends on it, and where its costs fall.

steps.label: Interpretation
steps.title: What starts to feel natural?
steps.description: Culture can teach people to treat an arrangement as necessary or deserved. Inherited expectations shape what they notice and accept.
steps.question: Separate the condition from the story that makes it seem inevitable.
steps.quote: A cultural lesson becomes an expectation; the expectation guides a decision; the decision helps teach the next person what to expect.

steps.label: Conduct
steps.title: Who has room to refuse?
steps.description: Authority and dependence create different possibilities for action. Accountability follows what someone knows, controls, and can realistically change.
steps.question: Examine a decision and its consequences, without assigning a fixed moral character to a class or group.
steps.quote: This is why the anatomy must record conduct as well as rank.

steps.label: Feedback
steps.title: What gets reproduced—or corrected?
steps.description: Decisions can defend the existing terms or make correction possible. Their effects become part of the conditions others encounter.
steps.question: Look for whether harm can be named, challenged, and repaired—and who can prevent that correction.
steps.quote: Our conduct then helps reproduce or change the arrangements shaping us.
steps.connection: What follows changes the next encounter

themes.label: The Leech
themes.title: Organized extraction.
themes.question: AMM’s name for the ownership, institutions, and claims that turn dependence into power over others. The model examines conduct and control.

themes.label: The Host
themes.title: A public with unequal power.
themes.question: People differ in resources, authority, and room to refuse. Responsibility follows what they can know, change, and choose to defend.

themes.label: The recovery
themes.title: Room to live differently.
themes.question: Independent judgment, accountability, rehabilitation, and parallel systems that people can inspect and correct.

chapters.line: The Leech is the attitude that treats domination of other people as a legitimate route to security, worth, or advantage.
Terms establish consequences. Explanations assign those consequences meaning. Repeated responses help teach which terms are open to question.
There is a threshold between learning that one must sometimes endure a condition and learning that the condition is right to impose.
A trustworthy revision supplies encounters in which another response is possible, can actually be taken, and does not return the old penalty under a new name.

money.definitionTitle: What is capital, in everyday language?

definitions.text: What you use to make a payment. A bank balance lets you buy something; by itself it does not tell you who owns the shop, the building, or the company.
What comes in over time: wages from work, interest from lending, or income from an asset. Your income pays today’s expenses. It is different from the wealth you already hold.

Here, money committed to an enterprise and assets used to generate income: equipment, buildings, software, or financial claims such as shares. Capital can expand what people can produce. Ownership also helps determine who controls it and receives the returns.
What you own minus what you owe. Two people with the same paycheck can have very different freedom to refuse a bad deal if one has savings and assets and the other has debt.

examples.title: The rent payment
examples.path: Tenant → property operator → costs, lender, owner
examples.mechanic: Rent is paid for access to a home. The recipient may pay for repairs, staff, taxes, insurance, and financing. What remains can benefit the owner. Paying rent ordinarily gives the tenant no ownership stake in the property.
examples.pressure: AMM’s concern is the leverage created when moving is costly and realistic alternatives are scarce. A person can keep paying for access while the asset—and the power to set future terms—remains someone else’s.
examples.question: Does the payment improve housing, or chiefly strengthen control over access to it?

examples.title: The debt payment
examples.path: Borrower → lender or loan owner → funding costs, losses, income
examples.mechanic: A loan lets you spend now against a promise to pay later. Principal repays the amount borrowed; interest is a separate charge. A lender also faces funding costs, administration, and the risk of nonpayment. The whole installment is not profit.
examples.pressure: When borrowing is needed for necessities, future income is already committed before it arrives. AMM focuses on terms that keep a person paying while leaving little room to reduce the debt or leave the arrangement.
examples.question: Does credit expand your choices—or keep your next paycheck spoken for?

examples.title: The platform fee
examples.path: Customer → seller → platform fees and operating costs
examples.mechanic: A seller may pay a platform for access to customers, payment processing, advertising, or delivery. These can be useful services. The platform’s receipts also pay its own costs before becoming profit.
examples.pressure: The leverage changes when sellers cannot readily reach buyers elsewhere and the platform controls visibility as well as price. AMM asks who does the work, who carries the risk, and who can change the fee or rules.
examples.question: Are you paying for a service—or for permission to reach the market?

examples.title: The public contract
examples.path: Public funds → contractor → delivery costs and profit
examples.mechanic: Governments buy goods and services from firms. A contract can fund useful work, wages, suppliers, and a return to the contractor. Public spending and private revenue are therefore connected.
examples.pressure: AMM examines arrangements in which necessity or emergency protects the contractor from effective challenge while the public bears costs and risk. A large contract alone does not establish that this happened.
examples.question: Who can inspect the cost, challenge the terms, and demand repair?

examples.title: The medicine price
examples.mechanic: A patent grants a period of exclusive sale to reward invention and risk. Public money often pays for part of the research: BARDA reimbursed 100 percent of Moderna’s allowable development costs for its COVID-19 vaccine.
examples.pressure: In Chapter Two’s words: “The problem is not the existence of intellectual property. It is the use of legal exclusivity to convert captive human need into pricing power.”
examples.question: Illness creates captivity. Who can refuse the price?

cycle.title: Control a necessity
cycle.text: Own or control housing, credit, infrastructure, or a route to customers.

cycle.title: Collect repeatedly
cycle.text: Charge for continued access, with terms that the dependent person struggles to refuse.

cycle.title: Expand the claim
cycle.text: Use returns, financing, or acquisitions to gain more assets and market power.

cycle.title: Protect the arrangement
cycle.text: Use contracts, influence, or rules to preserve the advantage. Test for this in each case.

money.testIntro: A strong critique follows the contract, the accounts, and the choices available. Use these questions on a company, a public institution, or an alternative that promises to replace them.

tests.title: What is actually being provided?
tests.text: Identify the work, investment, maintenance, and risk. Compare the charge with the service and its costs.

tests.title: What happens if someone says no?
tests.text: Look at switching costs, debt, scarcity, employment dependence, and available alternatives.

tests.title: Who receives the benefit and bears the loss?
tests.text: Trace ownership and the actual payments. Revenue, profit, wealth, and assets under management answer different questions.

tests.title: Who can change the terms?
tests.text: Find the decision-maker, the appeal route, and any evidence of retaliation, concealment, or blocked correction.

money.alternativeTitle: Build a different destination for the surplus.
money.alternativeDetail: Shared ownership can give the people using or operating an enterprise a say in its decisions. In a cooperative, members can direct surplus toward reserves, better services, member benefits, or agreed community purposes. It still has to cover costs, manage risk, and be answerable for its conduct.
money.movementDetail: 4Us is the founder’s movement toward economic sovereignty through cooperation; Sullix is its first platform test. The standard for that work should be concrete: clear ownership, visible costs, usable services, and an effective way to challenge decisions. These are goals to demonstrate as the work develops.
money.sourcesIntro: The explanations are complete on this page. The references below make the underlying definitions inspectable. AMM’s extraction model is an interpretation to examine; these sources do not establish its claims about any particular institution. The ownership figures carry their own sources and limits.

money.creditNote: This follows payments and ownership; it is not a model of the entire money supply. Bank lending can create deposits, and repaying bank-loan principal can reduce them. “Money moves” does not mean a fixed pile of cash simply passes from poor people to rich people.

companions.title: Who pays, who owns, who decides?
companions.text: Chapter Three’s anatomy of the Host distinguishes ordinary participation from the power to set the terms. Trace that difference through a rent payment, a loan, or a platform fee.
companions.summary: Examine how the logic of extraction can enter your judgment—and what you pass on to others.

companions.title: How does dependence become common sense?
companions.text: Chapter One examines the culture that makes power look legitimate. The money guide connects that argument to the recurring payments and ownership behind it.
companions.summary: Recognize how culture and public narratives teach you to accept the terms imposed on you.

companions.title: Put the anatomy next to an ordinary bill.
companions.text: Rent, interest, platform fees, and public contracts make the chapter’s “feeding interfaces” concrete. Follow the receipt, the costs, and the claim on what remains.
companions.summary: Follow your rent, debt, and platform fees into the institutions that collect them.

companions.title: Who owns the tools—and sets the price of using them?
companions.text: Read the letter alongside the platform example: technology can be useful while control over access gives its owners power over everyone who depends on it.
companions.summary: AI, ownership, and the people deciding who gains from the tools that others come to depend on.

companions.title: How does accumulated wealth become lasting authority?
companions.text: The ownership loop gives the letter’s critique a practical question: which claims on income and access are being carried forward, and who can challenge them?
companions.summary: A letter connecting the West’s history of domination to the ownership, dependency, and private power of the present.

capital.title: The new power is economic.
capital.intro: Who owns what you need? Who receives what you pay? AMM follows how ordinary payments can become concentrated private power—and how that power protects its position.
capital.mapIntro: Follow one ordinary payment, from the person who makes it to the power that collects it.
capital.mapLabel: The power map: concentrated private capital above the state, the guards and the story beneath it, and the citizen paying straight up.

tiers.label: The guards and the story
tiers.detail: Professionals who keep the arrangement beyond correction, and a culture that makes it seem natural

items.label: Lobbying, personnel, the systems it depends on

rail.label: Rent, interest, fees, data, attention
rail.note: Paid straight up, around the state

story.title: You pay.
story.text: Rent, a loan installment, a platform fee, a prescription. Each arrives as a separate bill, and each looks like a private problem.
story.quote: Each wound is returned to you as a separate personal deficiency while the environment producing the wounds remains unnamed.

story.title: The payment goes up.
story.text: Much of it never passes through the state. It runs straight to whoever owns the home, the debt, the platform, or the patent.
story.quote: A house cannot leave Denver, but the claim upon its rent can sit inside a national portfolio.

story.title: Capital collects.
story.text: At the top sits concentrated private capital. Chapter Two gives it two heads, security–industrial and technological–platform, and four mouths that feed them.
story.quote: The Leech appears where concentrated private power and captured public authority converge around something people cannot reasonably avoid, then convert that dependence into a recurring claim upon their labor, savings, attention, data, health, or future.

story.title: The state protects it.
story.text: The state still writes and enforces the rules. It is also a buyer: Lockheed Martin reported that 72 percent of its sales came from the U.S. government.
story.quote: The state is simultaneously its customer, financier, regulator, and protector.

story.title: The guards keep it beyond correction.
story.text: Between the rules and the person stand managers, lawyers, appraisers, and officials. Chapter Three does not fault the professions. It names a function.
story.quote: The guarding function appears when they use their discretion to keep an extractive arrangement beyond effective correction: concealing a known cost, discrediting a substantiated complaint, punishing an objection, or describing an avoidable injury as the necessary price of order.
story.source: Chapter Three · Class and the head of the Host

story.title: The story makes it feel natural.
story.text: In Chapter Two, what keeps the map from being questioned is not secrecy but the story told around it.
story.quote: Culture is not a fifth mouth. It is the tissue surrounding the entire organism. It teaches the host what to admire, what to tolerate, what to pursue, and what to consider inevitable.

capital.assaultIntro: Chapter Two names what the powers above command: organized force, computation, accumulated savings, and knowledge. Then it turns to the reader.

dot.title: AMM applies Digital Organism Theory to public life.
dot.intro: DOT distinguishes the experiencer from the Painting: the carried expectations, fears, skills, and meanings through which a situation is interpreted. AMM follows how these interpretations shape Intent and action, and how consequences become the next person’s experience.
dot.footer: An application of Digital Organism Theory.

links.title: The Experience Loop
links.quote: Every loop begins from the state left by earlier loops. This is why conditioning matters, and also why repeated truthful action can make a different response increasingly available.
links.applies: In AMM: an imposed condition becomes a learned expectation, an action, and then part of someone else’s environment.

links.title: The Fear-Gating Principle
links.quote: When Fear governs, the responses that feel available become fewer.
links.applies: In AMM: distinguish a refusal that feels unavailable from one made unaffordable by wages, debt, care, or institutional power.

links.title: Love as an Epistemic Condition
links.quote: Love is the condition in which Fear no longer governs you.
links.applies: In AMM: protect truthful participation, retain proportionate boundaries, and make authority capable of correction.
